entry: Young [[Female|female]] human, usually a [[Child|child]] or an adolescent. The term has other meanings, including young [[Woman|woman]], daughter or girlfriend regardless of age, but the first meaning is the most common one. The treatment and status of girls in a society is usually closely related to the status of women in that culture; where women have had a low social position, girls may be unwanted by their parents and society may invest less in them. Girls' formal education was traditionally considered far less important than boys'. In Europe, exceptions were rare before the printing press and the [[Reformation]] made literacy more widespread. One notable exception was [[Elizabeth I]] of England, who was educated in Latin, Greek, Spanish, French, philosophy, history, mathematics and music, an upbringing that has been argued to have helped her become a successful monarch.

Oil painting by Dutch Golden Age painter [[Johannes Vermeer]], dated c. 1665. It is a *tronie*, a 17th-century Dutch term for a "head" not meant to be a portrait, showing a girl in "exotic dress" and an "oriental turban". The sitter's identity is disputed. In 2014, astrophysicist Vincent Icke argued that the earring looks more like polished [[Tin|tin]] than [[Pearl|pearl]]. The painting has been held by the Mauritshuis in [[The Hague]] since 1902, when it was bequeathed to the museum. Its present title dates from the late 20th century.

Brazilian supermodel and activist. Born in Horizontina, Rio Grande do Sul, she has been one of the highest-paid models in the world since 2001. [[Forbes]] ranked her top of its highest-paid models list from 2005 to 2016. [[Vogue (magazine)|Vogue]] credited her with bringing the heroin chic era of modeling to an end in 1999. She was a Victoria's Secret Angel from 1999 to 2006 and has appeared on more than 1,200 magazine covers. She has been a Goodwill Ambassador for the United Nations Environment Programme since 2009.

Proprietary developer platform for creating, storing, managing, and sharing code. It uses Git for distributed version control and provides access control, bug tracking, task management, continuous integration, and wikis for every project. Headquartered in [[San Francisco]], it is operated by GitHub, Inc., a subsidiary of [[Microsoft]] since 2018. It is commonly used to host [[Open source|open-source]] software projects. As of January 2023 it reported over 100 million developers and more than 420 million repositories.

Collection of poems by the Bengali poet [[Rabindranath Tagore]]. The original Bengali collection, comprising 157 poems, was published on August 4, 1910, and many of its poems have been set to music as Rabindra Sangeet. Its central theme is devotion, and its motto is "I am here to sing thee songs" (Song No. XV). Tagore's own English translation, *Gitanjali: Song Offerings*, was published in November 1912 by the India Society of London and consists of 103 prose poems. Tagore received the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1913 for that English translation, making him the first non-European and the first Asian to receive it. The collection is part of the UNESCO Collection of Representative Works.

Italian general, revolutionary and republican. He contributed to the [[Unification of Italy|unification of Italy]] (the Risorgimento) and the creation of the [[Kingdom of Italy]]. Known as the "Hero of the Two Worlds" for his military campaigns in South America and Europe, he fought in the Ragamuffin War in Brazil and in the Uruguayan Civil War. In 1860 he led the Expedition of the Thousand, which conquered [[Sicily]] and southern Italy on behalf of Victor Emmanuel II, King of Sardinia. A unified Kingdom of Italy was created on March 17, 1861. He became an international figurehead for national independence and republican ideals, and is considered Italy's greatest national hero. His last campaign was during the [[Franco-Prussian War]], as commander of the Army of the Vosges. Admirers included [[Abraham Lincoln]], [[Victor Hugo]] and [[Charles Dickens]].

Italian composer, best known for his operas. Born near Busseto in the modern province of Parma, he came to dominate Italian opera after the era of [[Gioachino Rossini]], Vincenzo Bellini and Gaetano Donizetti. His early operas, beginning with *Nabucco* (1842), showed sympathy with the [[Unification of Italy|Risorgimento]]; its chorus "Va, pensiero" became identified with the unification movement, and Verdi was esteemed as a representative of its ideals. An intensely private person, he sought to establish himself as a landowner in his native region. His middle period produced *Rigoletto* (1851), *Il trovatore* and *La traviata* (both 1853). After *Aida* (1871) he returned with three late masterpieces: the *Requiem* (1874), *Otello* (1887) and *Falstaff* (1893). His operas remain among the most popular in the repertoire.

City in Greater Cairo, Egypt, on the west bank of the Nile opposite central Cairo. It is one of the world's most densely populated cities proper, with 45,300 inhabitants per square kilometer, and the third-largest city in Egypt by area and population. Giza is best known for the Giza Plateau, where the [[Great Pyramid of Giza]], the Great Sphinx and several other large pyramids and temples stand. It lies less than 30 km (20 miles) north of Memphis, the capital of the unified Egyptian state during the reign of [[Narmer|pharaoh Narmer]], roughly 3100 BC. In 2025 Giza was visited by 14.7 million [[Tourism|tourists]], making it the most popular tourist destination in Egypt, and its historic centre is listed as a [[World Heritage Site]].

Landform created by the action of [[Glacier|glaciers]]. Most of today's glacial landforms were created by the movement of large [[Ice sheet|ice sheets]] during the Quaternary glaciations, and some areas, such as Fennoscandia and the southern [[Andes]], have extensive examples. Erosional landforms include [[Cirque|cirques]], arêtes, glacial horns and U-shaped valleys, which become [[Fjord|fjords]] when filled with ocean water. Depositional landforms, left when retreating glaciers drop their glacial drift, include moraines, eskers and kames, and many are reshaped by meltwater into fluvioglacial landforms. Rare, very old fossil glacial landforms occur in the [[Sahara]].

Persistent body of natural ice, a form of rock, constantly moving under its own weight. A glacier forms where the accumulation of snow exceeds its ablation over many years, often centuries. It flows and deforms under the stresses of gravity and, as it moves, abrades the underlying rock to create landforms such as [[Cirque|cirques]], [[Moraine|moraines]] and [[Fjord|fjords]]. Distinct from the much thinner sea ice and lake ice, a glacier originates on land. About 99% of glacial ice lies in polar ice sheets, but glaciers occur in mountain ranges on every continent other than the Australian mainland. Glaciers cover about 10% of Earth's land surface, and [[Antarctica]]'s continental glaciers cover nearly 13 million km² (5 million sq mi). Glacial ice holds, together with ice sheets, about 69% of the world's freshwater, and glacial mass changes are considered among the most sensitive indicators of [[Climate change|climate change]].

Armed combatant in violent entertainments in the [[Roman Republic]] and [[Roman Empire]], fighting other gladiators, wild animals and condemned criminals. Most gladiators were slaves, schooled under harsh conditions, socially marginalized and segregated even in death, although some were volunteers who risked their legal and social standing. Fighting or dying well could bring them admiration and popular acclaim. Evidence of gladiatorial combat appears in funeral rites during the [[Punic Wars]] of the 3rd century BC. Early literary sources disagree on its origin, and some modern scholars favor a [[Campania|Campanian]] origin based on pictorial evidence. The games lasted nearly a thousand years, peaking between the 1st century BC and the 2nd century AD.

Genus of perennial cormous flowering plants in the iris family (Iridaceae), sometimes called the sword lily. The name comes from the Latin diminutive of *gladius*, a sword. The genus occurs in Asia, Mediterranean Europe, South Africa and tropical Africa, with its center of diversity in the Cape Floristic Region. About 260 species are endemic to southern Africa and about 10 are native to Eurasia. [[Carl Linnaeus]] first described the genus in 1753. The South African species were originally pollinated by long-tongued bees, but [[Sunbird|sunbirds]], hawk-moths and flies also pollinate them. Gladioli have been extensively hybridized, and the larvae of some [[Lepidoptera]] species, including the large yellow underwing, feed on them. As of August 2025, Plants of the World Online accepted almost 300 species and hybrids.

Cell or organ in an animal's body secreting substances into the bloodstream, a body cavity or an outer surface. Endocrine glands are ductless and secrete [[Hormone|hormones]] directly into interstitial spaces to be taken up into the bloodstream. They include the pineal gland, thymus, pituitary gland, [[Thyroid|thyroid]] and the two [[Adrenal gland|adrenal glands]]. Exocrine glands secrete their products through a duct onto a body cavity or outer surface, and are classified by method of secretion as merocrine, apocrine or holocrine, or by product as serous, mucous or sebaceous. Glands are mostly composed of [[Epithelium|epithelial]] tissue, typically with a supporting connective-tissue framework and a capsule.

Bulbous structure at the distal end of the [[Penis|penis]]. It is the most sensitive erogenous zone in the human male and the expanded cap of the corpus spongiosum, the spongy tissue surrounding the [[Urethra]]. It develops from the genital tubercle during embryonic life and is anatomically homologous to the clitoral glans in [[Female|females]]. Lined with mucosal tissue, it has an elastic band called the frenulum on its underside. In uncircumcised men it is covered by the foreskin, which in adults can generally be retracted over it.

City on the River Clyde in west central Scotland, the largest in Scotland (pop., 2020: 632,350). Grown from a small rural settlement near Glasgow Cathedral, it became the largest seaport in Scotland and the tenth-largest by tonnage in Britain. In the Victorian and Edwardian eras it was commonly called the "second city of the [[British Empire]]". Its population peaked at 1,127,825 in 1938, and urban renewal projects in the 1960s and 1970s relocated many residents to new towns. Glasgow became a major center of the Scottish Enlightenment in the 18th century and was European Capital of Culture in 1990. It is known for [[Association football|association football]], particularly the Old Firm rivalry, and it hosted the Commonwealth Games in 2014 and 2026.

Vision eyewear with clear or tinted [[Lens|lenses]] in a frame worn in front of the eyes. Corrective lenses bend light to correct refractive errors such as [[Myopia|nearsightedness]], farsightedness and [[Astigmatism|astigmatism]]. Presbyopia, a common condition in people over forty, is corrected with bifocal, trifocal or progressive lenses. Sunglasses are tinted or polarized to protect the eyes from bright light, and photochromic lenses darken in [[Ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] light. Safety glasses shield the eyes from debris and are worn in sports such as [[Squash (sport)|squash]] and [[Skiing|skiing]]. The earliest ancestors of modern glasses were 13th-century Italian "reading stones", magnifying spheres held over books. The temple arms that hook over the ears were not invented until the 1700s.

Group of eye diseases damaging the optic nerve. Often called the "silent thief of sight" because vision loss usually occurs slowly, it has a major risk factor in increased intraocular pressure, which is also associated with old age and family history. In open-angle glaucoma, drainage of aqueous humor is impeded; closed-angle glaucoma is a sudden blockage and an emergency. Treatment, typically eye drops, laser or [[Surgery|surgery]], aims to lower eye pressure. Glaucoma is a leading cause of blindness among [[African Americans]], and in 2013 its global prevalence among people aged 40–80 years was estimated at 3.54%.

American country musician and actor. A session guitarist in Los Angeles who played with the group later known as "The Wrecking Crew", he became a solo star with hits such as "Wichita Lineman" and "Rhinestone Cowboy". He released 64 albums, sold over 45 million records worldwide and won four [[Grammy Awards|Grammys]] in 1967. He hosted *The Glen Campbell Goodtime Hour* on [[CBS]] from 1969 until 1972. Campbell announced in 2011 that he had [[Alzheimer's disease]], and he retired in 2013 after recording his final song.

American actress and singer. Her career spans five decades on stage and screen, with three Primetime Emmy Awards, three Tony Awards, three Golden Globe Awards and eight [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] nominations. Her films include *The World According to Garp* (1982), *Fatal Attraction* (1987) and *Dangerous Liaisons* (1988). She won two consecutive Emmys for playing Patty Hewes in *Damages*. She is vocal on issues such as [[Women's rights|women's rights]], [[Same-sex marriage]] and [[Mental health]].

Canadian pianist and broadcaster, regarded as one of the greatest pianists of the 20th century. He was renowned as an interpreter of the keyboard works of [[Johann Sebastian Bach]] and rejected most Romantic piano literature in favor of Bach and Beethoven. His recordings also included Sweelinck, William Byrd and Orlando Gibbons, whom he called his favorite composer, and works by Schoenberg and Hindemith. He disliked public performance and stopped giving concerts at age 31 to concentrate on studio recording and media. He also produced television programs and radio documentaries about classical music. His recording of the Prelude and Fugue in C major (BWV 870) is on the [[Voyager Golden Record]].

American big band conductor, arranger and composer. His civilian band, Glenn Miller and his Orchestra, was the best-selling recording band from 1939 to 1942, with hits including "Moonlight Serenade" and "Chattanooga Choo Choo". In four years it scored 16 number-one records and 69 top-10 hits, more than [[Elvis Presley]] (40) or [[The Beatles]] (35). Miller enlisted in the US Army in 1942 and led an Army Air Forces orchestra that became the forerunner of many US military bands. He went missing over the [[English Channel]] during [[World War II]] when his flight from England to France never arrived. He was officially declared dead a year and a day later and was posthumously awarded the Bronze Star Medal.

Fixed-wing aircraft supported in flight by the dynamic reaction of air against its lifting surfaces, without reliance on an engine. Most gliders have no engine, although motor gliders carry small engines to extend their flight. Most exploit meteorological phenomena such as rising air to gain height, and gliders are principally used for gliding, [[Hang gliding|hang gliding]] and paragliding. Sir George Cayley's gliders achieved brief wing-borne hops from around 1849. Otto Lilienthal made repeated successful flights, eventually over 2,000, and was the first to use rising air to prolong them. The [[Wright brothers]] built three manned gliders before their powered flight. Sport gliding became the main application of gliders, and modern gliders regularly fly hundreds or even over a thousand kilometers in a day when the weather is suitable. Military gliders were developed during [[World War II]] for landing troops.

Terms for two groups of countries classified by socioeconomic characteristics, corresponding to developed and developing or least developed countries. According to UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD), the Global South comprises [[Africa]], Latin America and the Caribbean, Asia excluding Israel, Japan and South Korea, and Oceania excluding Australia and New Zealand. The Global North comprises Northern America and Europe, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand. The groups are not strictly geographical, since many Global South countries lie in the [[Northern Hemisphere]]. Global North countries tend to be wealthier and to export advanced manufactured products, while Global South countries are often poorer and depend on agrarian primary sectors. The term was introduced as a more open alternative to "Third World", and many Global South countries are current or former subjects of [[Colonialism|colonialism]].

Satellite-based [[Navigation|navigation]] system owned by the [[United States]] Space Force and operated by Mission Delta 31. It provides geolocation and time information to receivers anywhere on or near Earth where signal quality permits, and it does not require the user to transmit any data. The Department of Defense began the project in 1973, and the full constellation of 24 [[Satellite|satellites]] became operational in 1993. After Korean Air Lines Flight 007 was shot down, President [[Ronald Reagan]] made GPS available for civilian use in 1988. Civilian accuracy was limited by Selective Availability, a deliberate error, until a law ordered it disabled on May 1, 2000. Without it, GPS was accurate to about 5 meters (16 ft), and receivers using the L5 band are accurate to 30 centimeters (12 in).

City serving as a primary node in the global economic network. The term was popularized by sociologist Saskia Sassen in her 1991 book *The Global City: New York, London, Tokyo*. Criteria vary by source, but common features include headquarters of multinational companies, a globalized financial sector with a [[Stock exchange|stock exchange]], and an internationally linked transportation infrastructure. [[New York|New York City]], [[London]], [[Tokyo]] and [[Paris]] are the most commonly mentioned.
